# Working Papers

[From Reservation to Transformation: The Socioeconomic Impact of Political Quotas](pdf/Reservation_to_Transformation.pdf)   <br />
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; [[PDF](pdf/Reservation_to_Transformation.pdf)]

<p style="margin-top: -15px">
    <button class="abstract-btn">Abstract</button>
</p>
<div class="abstract-content">
The role of affirmative action policies in promoting socioeconomic mobility remains a subject of intense global debate, with countries implementing varying strategies to address historical inequalities. This study leverages India's 2008 delimitation exercise as a natural experiment to assess the impact of political quotas for Scheduled Castes (SCs) on local socio-economic outcomes, focusing specifically on SC outcomes within villages rather than solely village-level metrics. We find that SC reservations substantially increase SC student enrollment, particularly in prestigious schools, and foster entrepreneurial activity, as evidenced by the growth in both the number and size of SC-owned firms. Additionally, quotas facilitate SCs' entry into higher-status occupations, helping to erode entrenched caste-based occupational barriers.  These effects are driven by greater access to formal institutional funding for SC-owned firms and improvements in the quality of politicians elected under the quota system.  Improvements at the village level, including infrastructure enhancements and increased economic activity, further support these outcomes. Notably, the observed gains persist even after villages lose reserved status, underscoring the long-term benefits of these policies. Our findings contribute to the global discourse on affirmative action, suggesting that targeted, well-implemented quotas can yield sustained social and economic mobility for marginalised groups. With India's next delimitation scheduled post-2026, this research provides critical insights for policymakers worldwide seeking effective strategies to address inequality and social stratification.
</div>

[Ancient Epics in the Television Age: Religious Identity and the Rise of Hindu Nationalism in India](pdf/Ramayan.pdf), (with [Paul Brimble](https://pbrimble.github.io/), [Akhila Kovvuri](https://vpge.stanford.edu/people/akhila-kovvuri), [Alessandro Saia](https://sites.google.com/site/asaia9585/alessandro-saia) and [Dean Yang](https://deanyang-econ.github.io/deanyang/)) [NBER WP 33417](https://www.nber.org/system/files/working_papers/w33417/w33417.pdf)  <br />
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; Press: [The Hindu](https://www.thehindu.com/society/how-the-ramayan-tv-show-helped-shape-a-singular-nationwide-hindu-identity/article69202807.ece)

<p style="margin-top: -15px">
    <button class="abstract-btn">Abstract</button>
</p>
<div class="abstract-content">
The growing prominence of Hindu nationalism, known as "Hindutva," in India has garnered significant attention for its impact on politics and society, particularly its adverse effects on minority communities. However, the Hindu identity was not always a monolithic and political one. This study explores the potential role of a Hindu mythological show, "Ramayana," which aired on the solely available TV channel in India during 1987-88, in shaping the Hindutva identity primarily on the increasing salience of religious identity in people's political, social, and personal lives. We proxy for exposure to this show using location and television transmitters obtained from archival data and use signal propagation modelling based on irregular terrain to measure signal strength. Examining political and social manifestations of identity, we find that exposure to the TV show is associated with increased electoral success for right-wing Hindu nationalist parties, heightened tensions between Hindus and Muslims, and a decrease in the number of schools affiliated with the significant far-right Hindu nationalist organization. Our next steps involve investigating the impact on personal expressions of identity, such as child naming practices and dietary choices influenced by religious taboos.</div>


[Leader Marches as an Opposition Electoral Strategy](pdf/bharat_jodo_yatra.pdf), (with [Feyaad Allie](https://www.feyaadallie.com/) )  <br />
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; Press: [Hindustan Times](https://www.hindustantimes.com/india-news/bharat-jodo-yatra-boosts-congress-strike-rate-and-vote-share-in-karnataka-elections-101684006733079.html)

<p style="margin-top: -15px">
    <button class="abstract-btn">Abstract</button>
</p>
<div class="abstract-content">
Opposition parties struggle against populist incumbents who portray them as elite and out of touch, while often consolidating power to tilt electoral politics in their favor. How can the opposition respond? We conceptualize and examine leader-driven grassroots campaigns as an electoral strategy, focusing on the Indian National Congress leader Rahul Gandhi's 150-day Bharat Jodo Yatra. These campaigns aim to connect directly with voters and reshape the opposition's image. Using newly collected election data and a difference-in-differences design, we find that exposure to the yatra improved Congress’ performance, though in spatially and temporally limited ways. Interviews and descriptive evidence demonstrate how these campaigns can improve perceptions of the opposition. An original survey of 3500 voters reveals that those who directly participated in the grassroots campaign experienced longer-term positive impacts. The findings underscore the potential and the challenges of leader-driven grassroots campaigns as a mobilization strategy for opposition parties facing powerful populist incumbents.
</div>

[Technology and the Production of Justice: System-Wide Effects of Indonesia's E-Court Reform](pdf/ecourts_indonesia.pdf), (with [Sultan Mehmood](https://sites.google.com/view/sultan-mehmood/home) and Alexandra Filimonova)  <br />
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; [[PDF](pdf/ecourts_indonesia.pdf)]

<p style="margin-top: -15px">
    <button class="abstract-btn">Abstract</button>
</p>
<div class="abstract-content">
Delays in judicial proceedings are a pervasive institutional challenge. We study how technology changes judicial production using Indonesia's e-court reform, which introduced e-filing, e-payments, and virtual hearings for civil but not criminal cases. Using case-level data linking trial decisions to appeals, we compare civil and criminal cases handled by the same judge in the same court before and after reform. E-courts reduced case duration by about 7 days, or 15 percent, while preserving judicial quality. If anything, appeals and reversals fell, judgments became more concise, and readability and statutory citations were unchanged. The gains extended through the judicial system: case duration in untreated appellate courts fell by about 9 days, or 20 percent. The pattern is consistent with the reform freeing judicial capacity for more complex disputes, highlighting the potential for technology to expand capacity by reorganizing judicial production and relieving system-wide congestion.
</div>
